passed.title: Build a real Array column before calling Expr.arr methods
passed.trap: `pl.DataFrame` infers nested Python lists as `pl.List`, not `pl.Array`, as the printed schema `List(Int64)` shows. Calling `Expr.arr.sum` on such a column raises an error, because the `.arr` namespace expects a fixed-width `pl.Array` column. Declare the column as `pl.Array(inner, width)` in `schema=`, or convert an existing list column with `Expr.list.to_array`. For data whose length genuinely varies, use the `Expr.list` namespace instead.
passed.example:
import polars as pl

df = pl.DataFrame({"a": [[1, 2], [3, 4]]})
print(df.schema)  # inferred as List, not Array
try:
    df.select(pl.col("a").arr.sum())
    print("no error")
except Exception:
    print("raised: .arr needs an Array column")

# Fix 1: convert the list column to a fixed-width array
fixed = df.with_columns(pl.col("a").list.to_array(2))
print(fixed.schema)
print(fixed.select(pl.col("a").arr.sum()).to_dicts())

# Fix 2: declare the Array dtype up front
df2 = pl.DataFrame({"a": [[1, 2], [3, 4]]}, schema={"a": pl.Array(pl.Int64, 2)})
print(df2.select(pl.col("a").arr.sum()).to_dicts())
passed.output:
Schema({'a': List(Int64)})
raised: .arr needs an Array column
Schema({'a': Array(Int64, shape=(2,))})
[{'a': 3}, {'a': 7}]
[{'a': 3}, {'a': 7}]

passed.title: Expr.arr.get raises on out-of-bounds unless null_on_oob=True
passed.trap: Part of the `Expr.arr.get` docstring prose says an out-of-bounds index returns `None`. However, with the default `null_on_oob=False` it raises an error instead. If you expect a null for a missing position, pass `null_on_oob=True` explicitly. Negative indices count from the end, so `-1` gives the last element; `Expr.arr.last` expresses that more clearly.
passed.example:
import polars as pl

df = pl.DataFrame({"a": [[1, 2], [3, 4]]}, schema={"a": pl.Array(pl.Int64, 2)})

try:
    df.select(pl.col("a").arr.get(2))
    print("no error")
except Exception:
    print("raised: index out of bounds")

print(df.select(pl.col("a").arr.get(2, null_on_oob=True)).to_dicts())
print(df.select(pl.col("a").arr.get(-1)).to_dicts())
print(df.select(pl.col("a").arr.last()).to_dicts())
passed.output:
raised: index out of bounds
[{'a': None}, {'a': None}]
[{'a': 2}, {'a': 4}]
[{'a': 2}, {'a': 4}]

passed.title: Expr.arr.head, tail and slice return List by default, not Array
passed.trap: By default, `Expr.arr.head`, `Expr.arr.tail` and `Expr.arr.slice` return a `pl.List` column, even though the input is a fixed-width `pl.Array`. Chaining another `.arr` method onto that result then fails because the dtype is no longer Array. Pass `as_array=True` to keep a fixed-width Array; this requires constant `n`, `offset` and `length` values. Alternatively, continue with the `Expr.list` namespace.
passed.example:
import polars as pl

df = pl.DataFrame({"a": [[1, 2, 3], [4, 5, 6]]}, schema={"a": pl.Array(pl.Int64, 3)})

print(df.select(pl.col("a").arr.head(2)).schema)  # List
try:
    df.select(pl.col("a").arr.head(2).arr.sum())
    print("no error")
except Exception:
    print("raised: result is List, not Array")

print(df.select(pl.col("a").arr.head(2, as_array=True)).schema)  # Array
print(df.select(pl.col("a").arr.head(2, as_array=True).arr.sum()).to_dicts())
print(df.select(pl.col("a").arr.slice(1, 2, as_array=True)).to_dicts())
print(df.select(pl.col("a").arr.head(2).list.sum()).to_dicts())
passed.output:
Schema({'a': List(Int64)})
raised: result is List, not Array
Schema({'a': Array(Int64, shape=(2,))})
[{'a': 3}, {'a': 9}]
[{'a': [2, 3]}, {'a': [5, 6]}]
[{'a': 3}, {'a': 9}]

passed.title: Expr.arr.all and Expr.arr.any ignore null elements
passed.trap: `Expr.arr.all` and `Expr.arr.any` ignore null elements inside a sub-array rather than treating them as unknown. As a result, an all-null array gives `true` for `Expr.arr.all` and `false` for `Expr.arr.any`. Only a null array row itself produces null. If a null element should count against the result, count nulls with `Expr.arr.agg(pl.element().null_count())` and combine that check with `Expr.and_`.
passed.example:
import polars as pl

df = pl.DataFrame(
    {"a": [[True, True], [None, None], [False, None], None]},
    schema={"a": pl.Array(pl.Boolean, 2)},
)
nulls = pl.col("a").arr.agg(pl.element().null_count())
out = df.with_columns(
    all=pl.col("a").arr.all(),
    any=pl.col("a").arr.any(),
    nulls=nulls,
    all_no_nulls=pl.col("a").arr.all().and_(nulls.eq(0)),
)
print(out.columns)
for row in out.rows():
    print(row)
passed.output:
['a', 'all', 'any', 'nulls', 'all_no_nulls']
([True, True], True, True, 0, True)
([None, None], True, False, 2, False)
([False, None], False, False, 1, False)
(None, None, None, None, None)

passed.title: Expr.arr.join silently drops nulls by default
passed.trap: `Expr.arr.join` defaults to `ignore_nulls=True`, so null elements vanish from the joined string. For example, `["a", null]` becomes `"a"` with no hint that a value was missing. Pass `ignore_nulls=False` to make the whole result null whenever a sub-array contains a null. The method also errors if the inner dtype is not `pl.String`, so cast first with `Expr.cast`.
passed.example:
import polars as pl

df = pl.DataFrame(
    {"s": [["a", None], ["x", "y"]]},
    schema={"s": pl.Array(pl.String, 2)},
)
out = df.select(
    default=pl.col("s").arr.join("-"),
    strict=pl.col("s").arr.join("-", ignore_nulls=False),
)
print(out.to_dicts())

passed.title: Expr.arr.std and Expr.arr.var default to ddof=1 (sample statistics)
passed.trap: `Expr.arr.std` and `Expr.arr.var` default to `ddof=1`, which gives the sample estimator rather than the population statistic. Code that assumes `ddof=0` silently gets different numbers: for `[1, 2]` the default std is `0.7071` while `ddof=0` gives `0.5`. Pass `ddof=0` explicitly when you want the population statistic.
passed.example:
import polars as pl

df = pl.DataFrame({"a": [[1, 2], [4, 3]]}, schema={"a": pl.Array(pl.Int64, 2)})
out = df.select(
    std_default=pl.col("a").arr.std(),
    std_pop=pl.col("a").arr.std(ddof=0),
    var_default=pl.col("a").arr.var(),
    var_pop=pl.col("a").arr.var(ddof=0),
)
print(out.to_dicts())

passed.title: Expr.arr.unique returns an unordered List
passed.trap: `Expr.arr.unique` defaults to `maintain_order=False`, so the order of the distinct values is not guaranteed. Code that takes the "first unique" value can therefore give wrong results. The output is also a `pl.List`, not an Array, because the number of distinct values varies per row. Pass `maintain_order=True` for first-occurrence order, or sort explicitly, and use `Expr.list` methods on the result.
passed.example:
import polars as pl

df = pl.DataFrame({"a": [[3, 1, 3, 2]]}, schema={"a": pl.Array(pl.Int64, 4)})

ordered = df.select(pl.col("a").arr.unique(maintain_order=True))
print(ordered.schema)  # List, not Array
print(ordered.to_dicts())

sorted_unique = df.select(pl.col("a").arr.unique().list.sort())
print(sorted_unique.to_dicts())
print(ordered.select(pl.col("a").list.first()).to_dicts())
